claims.text: The superconducting transition temperature of high-entropy alloys is primarily governed by average electron-phonon coupling strength.
Increasing the fraction of heavy transition metals enhances electron-phonon coupling.
Heavy transition metals induce greater local lattice distortions in the alloy.
Increasing heavy-transition-metal content modifies the electronic density of states near the Fermi level.
The proposed starting material is a single-phase solid-solution alloy containing at least five elements at concentrations of at least 5 at.% each.
The intervention is a systematic substitution that increases Nb, Ta, or other heavy-transition-metal content while retaining a single-phase solid solution.
Most widely studied type-A HEA superconductors contain large amounts of Nb and Ta, making an Nb-Ta-rich matrix a precedent for the proposed baseline.
Increased heavy-transition-metal incorporation produces enhanced local lattice distortion and a modified Fermi-level density of states.
Heavy transition metals contribute additional d-electrons to the alloy.
Additional d-electrons and increased lattice strain enhance electron-phonon coupling.
Enhanced electron-phonon coupling raises the superconducting transition temperature.
Increasing the heavy-transition-metal fraction will produce a systematic, measurable increase in Tc relative to the lower-heavy-metal baseline.
Increasing the heavy-transition-metal fraction may increase the upper critical field relative to the baseline.
The proposed relationship applies only while the alloys remain single-phase solid solutions without significant segregation or inhomogeneity.
Phase segregation or microstructural changes could affect superconductivity independently of intrinsic electron-phonon coupling.
A disordered Ta-Nb-Ti-U-Hf HEA is a weak-coupling BCS type-II superconductor with Tc of 2.4 K and Hc2 of 6.4 T.
For a cited Zr-based HEA analogue series, Tc was interpreted as evolving mainly with valence electron count.

contradictions.description: An increase in Hc2 is presented only as a possible outcome, but the falsification rule can be read as treating absence of an Hc2 increase as falsifying. A non-mandatory prediction should not independently serve as a decisive falsifier.
